answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1925–2013 · Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, 1979–1990
answer.sourceLine: She said it on 10 October 1980, closing the Conservative Party Conference in Brighton — the passage sits on page 12 of the press release checked against delivery, held in the Thatcher papers at the Churchill Archive Centre and published in full by the Margaret Thatcher Foundation ↗. The words in her mouth were not her own: the line was drafted by her speechwriter, the playwright Sir Ronald Millar, as a pun on Christopher Fry’s 1948 verse play The Lady’s Not for Burning.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Speech to Conservative Party Conference (“The Reason Why”)
Thatcher MSS (Churchill Archive Centre): THCR — press release checked against delivery

source.excerpt:
And I hope that it will be followed by a winter of common sense. If it is not, we shall not be—diverted from our course.

To those waiting with bated breath for that favourite media catchphrase, the “U” turn, I have only one thing to say. “You turn if you want to. The lady’s not for turning.” I say that not only to you but to our friends overseas and also to those who are not our friends.
trail: The Margaret Thatcher Foundation’s transcript ↗ carries the passage verbatim, with the venue given as Brighton, the timing as 1430–1515, and the source as Thatcher MSS (Churchill Archive Centre): THCR.
BBC On This Day’s report from 10 October 1980 ↗ quotes the line in exactly the form that circulates today and describes the “widespread cheers” that met it.

Word histories’ newspaper-archive survey ↗ finds no use of the phrase before this speech, quotes an AP account in the Los Angeles Times of 10 October 1980 identifying the Fry pun the same day, and tracks the phrase becoming a general idiom in British papers by 23–24 October 1980.
Wikiquote ↗ lists it among Thatcher’s sourced quotations, dated 10 October 1980 — not in its Disputed or Misattributed sections.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Margaret Thatcher Foundation’s text, page 12. The stray em dash in “we shall not be—diverted” marks her delivery pause; the Foundation notes the press release “appears to have been checked against delivery.”

author.name: Margaret Thatcher
author.heading: Who was Margaret Thatcher?
author.bio: Margaret Hilda Thatcher (née Roberts) was Britain’s first woman Prime Minister and the longest-serving of the 20th century, in office from 1979 to 1990 and Conservative leader from 1975. A Soviet journalist’s nickname for her, the Iron Lady, stuck to a politics that made confrontation a method. The Brighton speech of October 1980 came at the bottom of a recession, with her own party pressing her to soften — and it is the moment the persona and the policy locked together.

misattribution.heading: The credit that gets left out
misattribution.intro: This one is genuine — Thatcher said it, on the record, in front of the Conservative Party Conference. What travels badly is who wrote it, what it is a joke about, and the punctuation.

items.tag: The real author of the words
items.why: The speech was written by the playwright and screenwriter Sir Ronald Millar (1919–1998), Thatcher’s speechwriter; the line is named as among his most famous contributions ↗, and the UK Speechwriters’ Guild calls him “the author of the line” ↗. His authorship was already being reported in the press that year — the Sydney Morning Herald of 1 December 1980 revealed that “behind this rather theatrical line in speech-making stands, in fact, a man of the theatre,” as quoted by word histories ↗.

items.scope: What the joke is actually about
items.why: “The lady’s not for turning” is a pun on the title of Fry’s 1948 verse play The Lady’s Not for Burning ↗ — a comedy about a woman accused of witchcraft. Wikipedia’s account of the speech adds that Thatcher herself missed the reference ↗, citing a 1988 Globe and Mail piece by Mark Lawson and Eric J. Evans’s Thatcher and Thatcherism. Treat that as a reported detail rather than something documented in her own hand.

The archival text has a full stop and quotation marks — “the ‘U’ turn, I have only one thing to say. ‘You turn if you want to. The lady’s not for turning.’” — per the Margaret Thatcher Foundation ↗. The circulating version substitutes a colon and adds an exclamation mark, as in the BBC’s report ↗. Every word is hers; only the pointing moves. (And it is bated breath, not “baited” — a spelling error that spreads with the quote.)

misattribution.truthLine: She really said it, in those words, at Brighton on 10 October 1980 — the transcript is public ↗. The credit that goes missing belongs to Ronald Millar.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: By the autumn of 1980 Thatcher’s government was deep in recession. Unemployment had risen to two million from 1.5 million the year before, and commentators — along with her own predecessor as Conservative leader, Edward Heath — were pressing for the “U-turn” that post-war British governments had reliably performed when the numbers turned ugly, as Wikipedia’s account of the speech sets out ↗. Unemployment would exceed three million before the recession ended in 1982.

The joke was the answer. Rather than argue the economics again, the speech refused the question in eleven syllables, and the refusal became the brand. The BBC reported it the same day ↗ as a defiant speech that also, less famously, conceded she was “profoundly concerned about unemployment.” Within a fortnight the phrase had escaped politics entirely — a Darlington paper used it about a Victorian toffee statue, a Chester resident about a council committee chairman.
context.detailsSummary: The play the pun came from
detailsBody: The Lady’s Not for Burning is a 1948 verse comedy by Christopher Fry (1907–2005), set in the Middle Ages, in which an accused witch, Jennet, wants to live and a war-weary soldier, Thomas Mendip, wants to die. John Gielgud toured it and took it to Broadway, where it opened at the Royale Theatre on 8 November 1950 with Richard Burton and Claire Bloom in the cast, per Wikipedia’s article on the play ↗.

The allusion was legible to the press immediately: an Associated Press account carried in the Los Angeles Times of 10 October 1980 already glossed the line as “a pun on the Christopher Fry play,” as word histories documents ↗.
context.pull: Millar expected the crowd-pleaser to be “You turn if you want to.” The headlines took the other half.

The lady's not for turning.” I say that not only to you but to our friends overseas..."; venue Brighton; editorial note 1430-1515 and "press release appears to have been checked against delivery"; source Thatcher MSS (Churchill Archive Centre): THCR; page carries "Copyright (c) Margaret Thatcher Foundation. Internet Archive snapshot (6 Aug 2026) of margaretthatcher.org/document/104431 — fetched and read in full; contains the verbatim passage, the Brighton venue, the 1430-1515 editorial note, the THCR archival source, and the Margaret Thatcher Foundation copyright notice.

BBC On This Day, 10 October 1980: reports the Brighton conference speech and quotes "To those waiting with bated breath for that favourite media catchphrase, the U-turn, I have only one thing to say: You turn if you want to. The lady's not for turning!"; also reports "widespread cheers", the two million unemployed, and her line "I am profoundly concerned about unemployment."

Wikipedia article on the speech: dated 10 October 1980, Conservative Party Conference; written by Sir Ronald Millar; a pun on the 1948 play The Lady's Not for Burning by Christopher Fry, "although Thatcher missed the reference herself" (cited to Mark Lawson, Globe and Mail, 18 Nov 1988, and Eric J. Evans, Thatcher and Thatcherism, 2004, p. 34); Millar intended "you turn if you want to" to be the most popular line; five-minute standing ovation; unemployment risen to 2 million by autumn 1980 from 1.5 million the previous year, exceeding 3 million by the time the recession ended in 1982; Edward Heath among those urging a U-turn.

Wikiquote lists the quotation in Margaret Thatcher's SOURCED quotations section (not Disputed or Misattributed), dated 10 October 1980 at a Conservative Party Conference, with the note that it is "A play on The Lady's Not for Burning, a 1948 play by Christopher Fry about a witchcraft trial."

Word histories (Pascal Treguer): the phrase "the lady's not for turning" originated in the speech written by Ronald Millar and delivered by Thatcher on Friday 10 October 1980 at the Conservative Party Conference in Brighton; quotes the passage from page 12 of the Margaret Thatcher Foundation text; quotes an Associated Press account in the Los Angeles Times of 10 October 1980 calling it "a pun on the Christopher Fry play 'The Lady's Not for Burning'"; notes Ronald Millar (1919-1998) as speech author per the Sydney Morning Herald of 1 December 1980 ("behind this rather theatrical line in speech-making stands, in fact, a man of the theatre"); earliest idiomatic reuses found in the Northern Echo, 23 October 1980, and the Chester Observer, 24 October 1980; Christopher Fry dated 1907-2005 and the play dated 1948.

Wikipedia: The Lady's Not for Burning is a 1948 play by Christopher Fry, a romantic comedy in verse set in the Middle Ages with an accused witch, Jennet, and a war-weary soldier, Thomas Mendip; first edition Oxford University Press, 1949; Broadway opening at the Royale Theatre 8 November 1950 with Richard Burton and Claire Bloom in the cast.

Wikipedia: Sir Ronald Graeme Millar (12 November 1919 - 16 April 1998) was an English actor, scriptwriter and dramatist and a Conservative Party speechwriter; "Among his most famous contributions for Thatcher was the line 'The lady's not for turning'."

UK Speechwriters' Guild page describes Ronald Millar as "the author of the line, 'The lady's not for turning', which was inspired by the title of a play, The Lady's Not for Burning by Christopher Fry." (The page does not address whether Thatcher understood the allusion.)

Wikipedia: Margaret Hilda Thatcher (13 October 1925 - 8 April 2013), Prime Minister of the United Kingdom 1979-1990 and Leader of the Conservative Party 1975-1990; first woman to hold the office; nicknamed the "Iron Lady".
